analysis.one_liner: Stops hospitals and doctors from sending patients surprise bills for out-of-network emergency and hospital care.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 30 bipartisan Senate cosponsors, but it never got a committee vote before the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: When you go to the emergency room or an in-network hospital, you can get billed by an out-of-network doctor who treated you without your choosing. This bill would have made that illegal: you would pay only your plan's normal in-network cost for those services, the insurer would pay the doctor the median in-network rate directly, and a neutral arbitrator would settle any payment dispute between the insurer and the provider. It also added transparency rules, like putting in- and out-of-network deductibles on insurance cards and requiring hospitals to disclose financial deals with physician groups. The bill was referred to the Senate health committee in May 2019 and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Privately insured patients. The bill's own findings note about 30 percent of insured Americans got a surprise medical bill in the past year, roughly 70 percent of patients billed by an out-of-network provider didn't know that provider was out-of-network, and a third of people struggling to pay a medical bill say it came from an out-of-network provider [S3]. Under the bill, patients would owe only in-network cost-sharing for emergency care and for out-of-network services at in-network facilities, and those payments would count toward their deductible and out-of-pocket maximum [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Patients could not be balance-billed beyond in-network cost-sharing for emergency services, for out-of-network providers working at in-network facilities, or for follow-up care after an ER visit, with narrow exceptions when a stabilized patient signs a written notice and cost estimate [S2][S3].

Insurers would pay the median in-network rate directly to the provider, and either side could take the dispute to a certified independent dispute resolution process, which picks the more reasonable of the two final offers based on local in-network rates and other factors [S2][S3].

The bill added transparency measures: insurance cards would list in-network and out-of-network deductibles, plans would have to give cost estimates for elective services within 48 hours, hospitals would disclose financial relationships with physician groups and itemize ancillary services, and plans would annually report out-of-network claims data to federal regulators [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Out-of-network providers, especially emergency-room physician staffing companies and hospitals, would lose the ability to charge patients beyond their insurer's in-network rates, and would have to accept median in-network payments or win more through arbitration. Insurers would bear the provider payments, which could feed into premiums; the bill itself required a study of the effect on premiums and deductibles [S3].

drawbacks.text: Capping out-of-network payment at the median in-network rate would cut revenue for emergency physicians and hospitals that currently rely on balance billing, and providers and some analysts warned that sharply lower payment rates could shrink access to on-call specialties in some areas — a concern the bill partially addressed through its arbitration option, which let providers seek rates above the median [S3].

The independent dispute resolution process would add new administrative machinery and cost for plans and providers — fees charged by the arbitrator would be paid by the losing party — and the bill required a government study of the process's administrative cost and its estimated impact on premiums and deductibles [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is large and well-documented: surprise bills hit roughly 30 percent of insured people in a year and are concentrated in emergencies, when patients have no choice of provider [S3]. The main costs — lower payments to some providers and new arbitration machinery — are real but narrower, and the bill's design (an arbitration path rather than a hard price cap) was aimed precisely at softening them. On balance this was a patient-protection bill with acknowledged provider-side costs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee in May 2019 and never received a markup or floor vote; it died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-LA) introduced the STOP Surprise Medical Bills Act on May 16, 2019, with 11 original bipartisan cosponsors including Sens. Bennet, Young, Hassan, Murkowski, Carper, Sullivan, Brown, Cramer, Cardin, Kennedy, and Casey [S3].

The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions; the action history shows no further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — before the 116th Congress ended [S5].

Despite that inaction, the bill carried 30 cosponsors split almost evenly between the parties (14 Democrats, 16 Republicans), and the bill's findings cited polling that 86 percent of Americans say protecting people from surprise medical bills is important [S4][S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Out-of-network providers and hospitals that profit from balance billing kept the status quo through the end of 2020, since no version of this bill advanced. Similar surprise-billing protections did eventually become law in a different vehicle at the very end of 2020, but this bill's 30-cosponsor bipartisan effort produced no vote of its own.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Balance-billing providers, until a later law passed

for.name: Sen. Bill Cassidy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban surprise balance billing and set up an arbitration process for provider-insurer payment disputes.

for.name: 30 Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan backing comparable to competing surprise-billing proposals.

against.name: Sen. Lamar Alexander
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee received the bill on referral but never scheduled a markup or vote on it; the bill sat with no action for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Physician staffing companies and provider groups
against.role: Emergency medicine staffing companies and medical associations
against.what_they_did: Ran an extensive public lobbying campaign in 2019 against proposals that set out-of-network payment benchmarks or capped balance billing, urging an arbitration-only approach instead.

sides.party_line_note: The bill itself was bipartisan — 14 Democratic and 16 Republican Senate cosponsors — but its fate rested with a Republican committee chair who never brought it to a vote.

industries.industry: Emergency physician staffing companies and out-of-network providers
industries.note: These providers earn money by billing patients beyond what insurers pay; the bill would end that practice and route payment through median in-network rates, letting providers pursue more only through arbitration. Their gain under the status quo is directly patients' loss in the form of surprise bills.
Hospitals would lose balance-billing revenue from emergency and ancillary care and would face new disclosure rules on physician profit-sharing and itemized ancillary services on bills.

Insurers would pay the median in-network rate directly to out-of-network providers instead of facing arbitrary charges, and out-of-network payments would count toward patients' in-network deductibles. In this bill the insurers' financial interest runs alongside patients', though insurers fund the payments that could pressure premiums.
The bill would create a certified class of independent dispute resolution entities to decide payment disputes, a new revenue stream, with fees paid by the losing party.
